summary: At 09:00 the invoice service began routing legacy-client traffic through a newly enabled adapter configuration, and within two minutes invoice creation errors rose from below 0.2% to 38%. The legacy-client adapter configuration omitted the region-header mapping that the modern-client adapter retained, and 97% of sampled failed requests lacked the region header required by the routing function. Database health indicators stayed within the prior week's normal range, and disabling the new configuration at 09:19 restored the error rate below 0.2% within three minutes. The evidence supports the missing region-header mapping in the legacy-client adapter configuration as the proximate cause; the CPU rise appears to be a correlate rather than a cause, and the 08:54 PDF rendering ticket predates the change and is unconnected by any evidence item.

claims.text: A new legacy-client adapter configuration was enabled for invoice service routing at 09:00.
Invoice creation errors rose from below 0.2% to 38% at 09:02, two minutes after the change.
The dominant failure signature was a missing region header: 97% of sampled failed requests lacked it.
The routing function requires the region header to process a request.
The legacy-client adapter configuration omitted the region-header mapping while the modern-client adapter retained it.
The missing region-header mapping in the new legacy-client adapter configuration caused the invoice creation error spike.
Database error rate, saturation, and replication lag remained within the previous week's normal range, so the database is not implicated.
Disabling the new legacy-client adapter configuration at 09:19 restored errors below 0.2% within three minutes.
Application CPU rose from 51% to 65% during the incident, a moderate increase that remained below saturation.
The CPU rise is more plausibly a downstream correlate of the elevated error/retry traffic than an independent cause; the evidence does not establish its direction.
The 08:54 customer-support ticket about a PDF rendering defect predates the change and no evidence links it to invoice creation failures.
The impact appears scoped to legacy-client traffic, since only the legacy-client adapter configuration lacked the mapping.

uncertainties.text: The remaining 3% of sampled failed requests are unexplained; they may be a second failure mode or background noise.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Error-code and message breakdown for the failures that did carry a region header, compared with the pre-09:00 baseline failure mix.

uncertainties.text: The direction of the CPU relationship is unresolved: the rise from 51% to 65% could be an effect of error handling and retries, or an independent contributor.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: CPU time series aligned minute-by-minute with the error rate across 09:00-09:22, plus profiling or request-volume data showing whether retries drove the load.

uncertainties.text: Why the legacy-client adapter configuration omitted the region-header mapping is unknown (authoring error, intentional removal, or template/default gap).
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The change record and diff for the adapter configuration, with its review and approval history.

uncertainties.text: Whether any invoice creation failures were silent, partial, or produced duplicate or corrupt records is unknown.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Reconciliation of invoice records created between 09:00 and 09:22 against upstream request logs.

uncertainties.text: Whether the 08:54 PDF rendering defect shares any component with the invoice routing path is unknown; the evidence only gives its timestamp and subject.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The ticket's affected-component and stack-trace details, and whether the PDF path reads the region header.

uncertainties.text: Whether the same missing-mapping pattern exists in other configurations not covered by this evidence is unknown; only legacy-client and modern-client adapters are described.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: An inventory of all adapter configurations checked for the region-header mapping.

uncertainties.text: The detection and decision timeline between 09:02 and the 09:19 disable is not described, so the 17-minute gap cannot be attributed.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Alerting timestamps and the responder action log for that interval.

uncertainties.text: The absolute customer impact (number of failed invoices, affected accounts) is not given, only the error percentage.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Request volume for the incident window and the identities of the affected legacy clients.

actions.text: Add the region-header mapping to the legacy-client adapter configuration to match the modern-client adapter, and re-enable only after verifying the header is present end to end.
Make the routing function fail loudly and explicitly on a missing region header, with an error signature that names the missing field, so the same defect is diagnosable in seconds.
Audit every adapter configuration for required-field mappings, including the region header, rather than treating this as a single-configuration fix.
Gate configuration changes of this kind behind a staged rollout with an automatic error-rate abort, so a 38% error rate cannot persist for 19 minutes.
Reconcile invoices attempted between 09:00 and 09:22 to identify affected legacy clients and confirm no partial or duplicate records were created.
Triage the 08:54 PDF rendering ticket separately; keep it out of this incident's causal account unless component evidence links them.

counterfactuals.text: Had the legacy-client adapter configuration included the region-header mapping, the routing function would have received the header it requires and the error spike would very likely not have occurred.
Had the new configuration not been enabled at 09:00, errors would have stayed near the pre-change baseline, as shown by the return below 0.2% once it was disabled.
Had the change been rolled out to a small fraction of legacy-client traffic first, the blast radius would have been far smaller than 38% of invoice creations.
Had the database been the cause, disabling the adapter configuration would not have resolved the errors within three minutes, and database indicators would not have stayed normal.
Had application CPU been the cause, disabling the adapter configuration would not by itself explain recovery, and a rise to only 65% is weak grounds for a 38% failure rate.
Had the PDF rendering defect been causal, errors would have been expected to rise from 08:54 rather than at 09:02, immediately after the configuration change.
